text:
紫のふわふわロボットの動画が、
約175万回見られています。

作ったのは、
アメリカのDynamic Creaturesです。

CEOは、
ボストン・ダイナミクスで戦略責任者だった人です。

10月16日に、人と触れ合うロボット「Hugo」を発表しました。

既存のロボットをもとにしたキャラクターは、
リースで借りられます。

導入にかかるのは数か月だそうです。

テーマパークが借りられるなら、
着ぐるみとの分担が変わるかもしれません。

quotedTweet.text:
Introducing Hugo: the first human companion robot.

At Boston Dynamics, I was Chief Strategy Officer, bringing robots into the real world.

My co-founder, Farbod Farshidian, led research at the RAI Institute.

Together, 15+ years teaching robots to run, jump, and work.

So we asked: what if robots could connect with people?

Hugo runs on the first Vision-Language-Expression (VLE) model.

He links what he sees and hears to movement, expression, and gesture.

He notices you, reads the room, and reacts in real time.

And he's only the first.

Dynamic Creatures is @BostonDynamics' official entertainment and hospitality partner.

We're building a cast of characters with film studios, resorts, and theme parks.

text:
Most robots treat people like furniture to dodge.  

Hugo flips the script. Humans become signals worth responding to, noticed, read, answered in real time.

Giving robots personality and expression is just fascinating. 

Those small reactions are what make a character feel alive.

That’s a genuinely appealing direction for social robots, especially the ones meant to live among us in parks, hotels, and resorts.

The real test isn’t the first high-five or hug. It’s whether the interaction still feels good after the novelty fades.

Wrap the robotics in a friendly, funny, or other designs...and this can have such a positive effect on the world and people 🩵

Introducing Hugo: the first human companion robot.

At Boston Dynamics, I was Chief Strategy Officer, bringing robots into the real world.

My co-founder, Farbod Farshidian, led research at the RAI Institute.

Together, 15+ years teaching robots to run, jump, and work.

So we asked: what if robots could connect with people?

Hugo runs on the first Vision-Language-Expression (VLE) model.

He links what he sees and hears to movement, expression, and gesture.

He notices you, reads the room, and reacts in real time.

And he's only the first.

Dynamic Creatures is @BostonDynamics' official entertainment and hospitality partner.

We're building a cast of characters with film studios, resorts, and theme parks.

text:
An ex-Boston Dynamics Chief Strategy Officer introduced Hugo, billed as the first human companion robot: purple, furry, horned, built to walk hotels and theme parks answering questions and handing out hugs

Dynamic Creatures is Boston Dynamics' official hospitality and entertainment partner, and the launch ran on Boston Dynamics' own site. The founder's read of the market: today's robots look like they walked out of a sci-fi movie, and that keeps people from welcoming them

The rest of the humanoid race sells labor. 1X opened pre-orders for NEO, a $20,000 home robot (or $499 a month) shipping to US homes in 2026 to learn chores. Hugo walks hotel lobbies and hands out hugs

1X's NEO learns chores through teleoperation, while Hugo answers questions and hugs guests. Both pitch the robot that lives with humans. Which definition of companion wins?

text:
I grew up watching animatronics. They were magic, and they ran the same loop forever. They never saw you.

Dynamic Creatures changed that. 

These robots read the room and respond to the person standing in front of them, in real time.

The team that taught Atlas how to walk brought in puppeteers to teach these robots emotion.

Most of the robotics money goes to factories. This team is building robots you actually meet.

I like it.

text:
Dynamic Creatures just unveiled Hugo, a furry character robot built to mingle with guests. Here's what you need to know.

Hugo is billed as the first human companion robot, and the company's first living character robot. Co-founder Marc Raibert-backed team Dynamic Creatures announced him on Oct 16, 2026. The launch post came from Marc Ermann, a former Chief Strategy Officer at Boston Dynamics. His co-founder, Farbod Farshidian, led research at the RAI Institute. Together they have 15+ years teaching robots to run, jump, and work. The post is marked as a paid partnership.

Hugo is a furry purple Tyrolean mountain troll. Reports say he is a bipedal robot with 57 joints and 43 devices that turn power into motion. He walks around the company's Boston office, dances, and high-fives people. The founders say they will never make one that looks human.

He runs on the first Vision-Language-Expression (VLE) model. It links what he sees and hears to movement, expression, and gesture. He notices you, reads the room, and reacts in real time. The robot runs on SnowJay, the company's integrated AI and robotics operating system, which coordinates how robots move, perceive, and respond.

The pitch is hospitality and entertainment. Dynamic Creatures is Boston Dynamics' official entertainment and hospitality partner. It is building a cast of characters with film studios, resorts, and theme parks. Commentators note that robotics startups raised a record $18.6 billion in one quarter this year, mostly for factories, warehouses, and defense. This company is going after guest spaces instead.

Key numbers:
- 15+ years of combined robotics experience across the two founders
- 57 joints and 43 motorized devices in Hugo
- $6.3M raised, from Eniac Ventures, Kindred Ventures, Bluegrass Ventures, Heliad, Sunshine Lake, and others
- $18.6B raised by robotics startups in one quarter
- 306K+ views on the launch post within hours

Hugo is only the first character, and more are planned for parks, hotels, and screens.

Introducing Hugo: the first human companion robot.

At Boston Dynamics, I was Chief Strategy Officer, bringing robots into the real world.

My co-founder, Farbod Farshidian, led research at the RAI Institute.

Together, 15+ years teaching robots to run, jump, and work.

So we asked: what if robots could connect with people?

Hugo runs on the first Vision-Language-Expression (VLE) model.

He links what he sees and hears to movement, expression, and gesture.

He notices you, reads the room, and reacts in real time.

And he's only the first.

Dynamic Creatures is @BostonDynamics' official entertainment and hospitality partner.

We're building a cast of characters with film studios, resorts, and theme parks.

It’s the first serious attempt to bring top-tier robotics into entertainment instead of factories.

Hugo from Dynamic Creatures is a prototype intended as the first in a series of robots designed to interact with humans in everyday settings.

Most robots register a person as an obstacle to slow down for. Hugo is built to treat your face, voice and movement as the input that drives what it does next.

text:
Boston Dynamics spinout Dynamic Creatures is introducing robot characters designed to roam theme parks, hotels and resorts and interact with guests in real time.

Its SnowJay AI platform coordinates how the robots move, perceive their surroundings and respond. 

The team uses motion capture and reinforcement learning to teach natural movement, with professional puppeteers helping shape the characters’ expressions.

The goal is for each character to adapt to the person in front of it as the interaction unfolds.

Dynamic Creatures is Boston Dynamics’ official hospitality and entertainment partner. 

 https://t.co/GMnOyye6CE

text:
A guy spent five years at Boston Dynamics, then quit to build a furry troll robot that strangers can't stop hugging.

It has 43 motors inside, walks around their Boston office, dances, high-fives people, and he swears he will never make one that looks human.

Marc told the Boston Dynamics CEO on day one that he only took the job to learn how to build companion robots later. He left and named the new company Dynamic Creatures, half Boston Dynamics, half Jim Henson's Creature Shop. The name tells you what he's building. Boston Dynamics engineering wearing a puppet's face.

Back in 1970 a Japanese roboticist named Masahiro Mori drew a curve. The closer a machine looks to human, the more people recoil, right up until you can't tell the difference. Fifty-six years later nobody has made it across. Humanoid startups keep walking into that dip with a chrome skeleton and a blank faceplate, and Hugo just goes around it with big eyes and fur.

Henson figured this out in 1979 with felt and a forearm. Kids hug Elmo on sight. I have never once seen anyone hug a $16,000 steel humanoid.

He's selling to everyone Disney won't. Disney built the BDX droids for its own parks, they wander Disneyland's Galaxy's Edge every day, and Disney is never renting them to a Marriott. Which means every cruise ship and casino that isn't Disney has had no way to put a walking character on the floor until now, and one company with an official Boston Dynamics partnership just showed up to be the vendor for all of them.

The operator math is where it gets fun. A performer in a full fur suit works short rotations with mandatory breaks once it gets hot. The robot never overheats, and a park can lease it instead of buying it.

The Vision-Language-Expression model is where this gets hard. Atlas did a backflip back in 2017. Noticing a nervous six-year-old and softening your wave turns out to be the harder trick, and it's the one that decides whether a character gets hugged or avoided.

Funny that after fifteen years on robots that jump, his first product is mostly about eye contact.

we spent 15 years teaching robots to run, jump, and do backflips

every robot ever built has been deaf and mute. can't see you. can't hear you. can't respond to you

hugo runs on a vision-language-expression model — he reads the room and reacts in real time

the team that gave atlas its walk is now teaching robots to feel

this is a massive shift

text:
Robotics startups raised a record $18.6 billion in one quarter this year, and almost all of it is going to factories and warehouses.

@dynamicreatures is going the other way. The team left Boston Dynamics to build character robots for theme parks and hotels. 

The robots read what's happening around them and respond to the person in front of them, instead of repeating the same loop like an animatronic.

The CTO helped give Atlas its natural walk. Marc Raibert is an angel investor.

If robots stop being built only to work, what's the first place you'd want to meet one?

the team that left Boston Dynamics went the other way and built characters you actually walk up to and meet

motion capture and reinforcement learning for the movement, professional puppeteers for the emotion

my brain genuinely refuses to accept there's a machine under there

quotedTweet.text:
Introducing Hugo: the first human companion robot.

At Boston Dynamics, I was Chief Strategy Officer, bringing robots into the real world.

My co-founder, Farbod Farshidian, led research at the RAI Institute.

Together, 15+ years teaching robots to run, jump, and work.

So we asked: what if robots could connect with people?

Hugo runs on the first Vision-Language-Expression (VLE) model.

He links what he sees and hears to movement, expression, and gesture.

He notices you, reads the room, and reacts in real time.

And he's only the first.

Dynamic Creatures is @BostonDynamics' official entertainment and hospitality partner.

We're building a cast of characters with film studios, resorts, and theme parks.
